meta.subject: Integrated Science & Physics (NaCCA Primary/JHS & Cambridge IGCSE/AS)
meta.topic: MeasurementLab v1.4.0 Verification (15 slides, 15 instruments & skills)

slides.title: 1. Primary Ruler — Measuring a Cocoa Pod
slides.purpose: NaCCA B5 length measurement using a centimetre ruler.
onScreenText: Align the object with the 0 cm mark
Read to the nearest 0.1 cm

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="225" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Primary Ruler — Length Measurement</text></svg>

narration.script: Read the length of the cocoa pod from the centimetre ruler.

keyIdeas: A standard school ruler has 1 mm (0.1 cm) smallest divisions.

interactive.title: Measure the Length of a Cocoa Pod
interactive.instructions: Inspect the ruler scale and enter the length of the cocoa pod with its unit.
interactive.fallbackText: The cocoa pod measures 12.4 cm on a 0–15 cm ruler with 0.1 cm divisions.
hints: Count whole centimetres first, then count the smaller 0.1 cm (1 mm) marks.

slides.title: 2. Primary Thermometer — Accra Midday Temperature
slides.purpose: NaCCA B5 temperature reading in degrees Celsius.
onScreenText: Liquid expands as temperature rises
Read the top of the liquid column at eye level

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#fef2f2"/><text x="400" y="225" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#7f1d1d">Primary Thermometer — Temperature (°C)</text></svg>

narration.script: Read the air temperature in Accra from the Celsius thermometer.

keyIdeas: Degrees Celsius (°C) is the standard everyday temperature scale.

interactive.title: Read the Courtyard Air Temperature
interactive.instructions: Read the temperature shown on the Celsius thermometer.
interactive.fallbackText: The thermometer reads 32 °C on a 0–50 °C scale.
interactive.successExplanation: 32 °C is a typical warm midday temperature in Accra.

slides.title: 3. JHS Measuring Cylinder — Concave Water Meniscus & Parallax
slides.purpose: NaCCA B7 volume measurement with concave meniscus and eye-level parallax alignment.
onScreenText: Water forms a concave meniscus in glass
Align eye level (0°) with the bottom of the meniscus

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#eff6ff"/><text x="400" y="225" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#1e3a8a">Measuring Cylinder — Concave Meniscus</text></svg>

narration.script: Move your eye level to zero degrees so there is no parallax error, then read the bottom of the concave water meniscus.

keyIdeas: Reading from above or below introduces parallax error.

commonMisconceptions: Reading the top edge of water meniscus

interactive.title: Measure Water Volume Without Parallax Error
interactive.instructions: Set eye level to 0° first, then read the bottom of the concave meniscus in mL.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Measuring cylinder water concave meniscus simulation
interactive.fallbackText: At eye level (0°), the bottom of the concave water meniscus sits at 46 mL.

prediction.prompt: For water in a glass measuring cylinder, which part of the meniscus should you read?
prediction.explanation: Water adheres to glass and curves downwards; read the lowest point of the meniscus at eye level.

interactive.successExplanation: 46 mL (or 46 cm³) read at 0° eye level avoids parallax error.

slides.title: 4. Measuring Cylinder — Convex Mercury Meniscus
slides.purpose: Demonstrate that not all liquids form concave menisci (mercury forms a convex meniscus).
onScreenText: Cohesive forces in mercury exceed adhesion to glass
Read the TOP of a convex meniscus

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f1f5f9"/><text x="400" y="225" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#334155">Convex Meniscus — Mercury Simulation</text></svg>

narration.script: Mercury forms an upward-curving convex meniscus. Read the highest central point at eye level.

keyIdeas: Read the top of a convex meniscus (e.g. mercury) and the bottom of a concave meniscus (e.g. water).

interactive.title: Read the Top of a Convex Mercury Meniscus
interactive.instructions: Inspect the convex meniscus at eye level and record the volume in mL.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Measuring cylinder convex mercury meniscus simulation
interactive.fallbackText: The top of the simulated convex mercury meniscus aligns with 28.5 mL.

slides.title: 5. JHS Balance — Mass Measurement with Tare (Mass vs Weight)
slides.purpose: NaCCA B8 laboratory balance with tare/zeroing and explicit mass vs weight distinction.
onScreenText: A balance measures MASS (g or kg), not WEIGHT (N)
Press Tare to zero out an empty beaker before weighing

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f0fdf4"/><text x="400" y="225" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#14532d">Laboratory Balance — Mass & Tare</text></svg>

narration.script: Press Tare to remove the beaker offset, then record the mass of the cassava sample in grams.

keyIdeas: Mass is measured in grams or kilograms; weight is a force measured in Newtons.

interactive.title: Tare the Balance and Measure Sample Mass
interactive.instructions: Press Tare/Zero to subtract the 34.2 g beaker, then record the cassava mass with its SI unit.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Digital laboratory balance with tare control
interactive.fallbackText: After taring the 34.2 g beaker, the cassava sample mass is 145.6 g.
interactive.successExplanation: 145.6 g (0.1456 kg) is a mass, not a weight in Newtons.

slides.title: 6. Digital Laboratory Balance — Resolution Uncertainty
slides.purpose: Demonstrate digital instrument reading and ±1 least-count uncertainty convention.
onScreenText: Digital instruments commonly take ±1 least count as resolution uncertainty

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#ecfeff"/><text x="400" y="225" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#155e75">Digital Balance — Resolution Uncertainty</text></svg>

narration.script: Read the digital analytical balance and state both the mass and its ±1 least-count uncertainty.

keyIdeas: A 0.01 g digital balance has ±0.01 g resolution uncertainty.

interactive.title: Record Digital Balance Reading and Uncertainty
interactive.instructions: Enter the mass to 2 decimal places and its ±1 least-count uncertainty.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Digital analytical balance with uncertainty check
interactive.fallbackText: The digital balance displays 24.35 g ± 0.01 g.

slides.title: 7. JHS Stopwatch — Resolution vs Human Reaction Time
slides.purpose: NaCCA B8 / IGCSE stopwatch timing distinguishing 0.01 s display resolution from ±0.2 s human reaction time.
onScreenText: A stopwatch displays 0.01 s, but human reaction time is ~0.2 s
Time multiple swings to reduce percentage uncertainty

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#fffbeb"/><text x="400" y="225" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#92400e">Stopwatch — Resolution vs Reaction Time</text></svg>

narration.script: Record the simulated stopwatch reading and its human reaction-time uncertainty of 0.2 seconds.

keyIdeas: Human reaction time (~0.2 s) dominates over a digital stopwatch's 0.01 s display resolution.

interactive.title: Record Stopwatch Time & Reaction-Time Uncertainty
interactive.instructions: Record the simulated elapsed time (s) and include the ±0.2 s human reaction-time uncertainty.
interactive.fallbackText: Simulated stopwatch reading: 14.8 s ± 0.2 s (human reaction-time uncertainty).

slides.title: 8. IGCSE Vernier Callipers — Brass Rod Diameter
slides.purpose: Cambridge 0625 vernier callipers reading from main scale + aligned vernier division.
onScreenText: Observed = Main Scale + (Aligned Vernier Division × 0.1 mm)

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="225" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">IGCSE Vernier Callipers (LC = 0.1 mm)</text></svg>

narration.script: Combine the main scale reading with the aligned vernier division to find the brass rod diameter in millimetres.

keyIdeas: 10 vernier divisions matching 9 mm gives a least count of 0.1 mm.

commonMisconceptions: Reading main scale at the edge of the jaw instead of the 0 mark

interactive.title: Read the Vernier Callipers (No Zero Error)
interactive.instructions: Read the main scale and aligned vernier division to determine the diameter in mm.
interactive.fallbackText: Main scale 23 mm + aligned vernier division 7 × 0.1 mm = 23.7 mm.

slides.title: 9. IGCSE Micrometer Screw Gauge — Half-Millimetre Sleeve
slides.purpose: Cambridge 0625 micrometer with 0.5 mm sleeve division visible and 50-division thimble.
onScreenText: Check if the 0.5 mm mark on the sleeve is visible!
Reading = Sleeve + (Thimble × 0.01 mm)

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#fffbeb"/><text x="400" y="225" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#78350f">IGCSE Micrometer Screw Gauge (0.01 mm)</text></svg>

narration.script: Notice the half-millimetre mark is visible on the sleeve. Add the thimble reading to get the wire diameter.

keyIdeas: Missing the 0.5 mm mark causes a 0.50 mm systematic error.

commonMisconceptions: Forgetting to add the visible 0.5 mm mark

interactive.title: Read a Micrometer with Visible 0.5 mm Sleeve Mark
interactive.instructions: Combine the sleeve reading (including 0.5 mm) and thimble division to 2 decimal places.
interactive.fallbackText: Sleeve 4.5 mm + thimble division 28 × 0.01 mm = 4.78 mm.

slides.title: 10. Positive Zero-Error Correction (Vernier Callipers)
slides.purpose: Diagnose and subtract a positive zero error (+0.2 mm).
onScreenText: Closed jaws read +0.2 mm
Corrected = Observed − (+0.2 mm)

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#fef2f2"/><text x="400" y="225" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#991b1b">Positive Zero-Error Correction</text></svg>

narration.script: First click Check Zero Error to see the positive zero offset, then subtract it from the observed reading.

keyIdeas: A positive zero error makes readings too large, so you must SUBTRACT it.

commonMisconceptions: Adding a positive zero error instead of subtracting

interactive.title: Correct a Positive Zero Error (+0.2 mm)
interactive.instructions: Inspect closed jaws for zero error, read the observed value (18.6 mm), and enter the corrected diameter.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Vernier callipers positive zero error simulation
interactive.fallbackText: Observed 18.6 mm minus +0.2 mm zero error = 18.4 mm.

slides.title: 11. Negative Zero-Error Correction (Micrometer)
slides.purpose: Diagnose and correct a negative zero error (−0.03 mm).
onScreenText: Closed anvil reads −0.03 mm
Corrected = Observed − (−0.03 mm) = Observed + 0.03 mm

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#eef2ff"/><text x="400" y="225" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#312e81">Negative Zero-Error Correction</text></svg>

narration.script: Inspect the negative zero error of minus 0.03 mm and add 0.03 mm to the observed micrometer reading.

keyIdeas: Subtracting a negative zero error adds its magnitude to the observed reading.

interactive.title: Correct a Negative Zero Error (−0.03 mm)
interactive.instructions: Check zero error, read the observed micrometer reading (6.22 mm), and enter the corrected thickness.

slides.title: 12. Analogue Ammeter — Selectable Current Ranges
slides.purpose: Cambridge 0625 analogue ammeter reading with 0–0.6 A and 0–3 A ranges.
onScreenText: Ammeters measure electric current in Amperes (A)
Always read the scale matching the connected terminal range

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#ecfeff"/><text x="400" y="225" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#164e63">Analogue Ammeter — Current (A)</text></svg>

narration.script: Select the 0 to 0.6 ampere range for higher precision and read the circuit current.

keyIdeas: Choosing the smallest range above the current gives better precision.

commonMisconceptions: Reading the 3 A scale when connected to 0.6 A terminal

interactive.title: Read the Analogue Ammeter (0–0.6 A / 0–3 A)
interactive.instructions: Inspect the active range and record the electric current with its unit (A or mA).
interactive.fallbackText: On the 0–0.6 A range, the ammeter needle points to 0.42 A (420 mA).

slides.title: 13. Analogue Voltmeter — Potential Difference
slides.purpose: Cambridge 0625 analogue voltmeter distinguishing potential difference (V) from current (A).
onScreenText: Voltmeters measure potential difference in Volts (V)
Connected in parallel across a component

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#faf5ff"/><text x="400" y="225" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#581c87">Analogue Voltmeter — Potential Difference (V)</text></svg>

narration.script: Read the potential difference across the resistor on the 0 to 15 volt range.

keyIdeas: Potential difference is measured in Volts (V), not Amperes (A).

interactive.title: Read the Analogue Voltmeter (0–15 V Range)
interactive.instructions: Record the potential difference across the resistor with its unit (V).
interactive.fallbackText: On the 0–15 V range, the voltmeter reads 9.5 V.

slides.title: 14. Repeated Measurements, Mean & Half-Range Uncertainty
slides.purpose: Cambridge IGCSE/AS repeated trial recording, mean calculation, and half-range uncertainty.
onScreenText: Record 3 repeated trials
Mean = (t₁ + t₂ + t₃) / 3
Half-range uncertainty = (max − min) / 2

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f0fdfa"/><text x="400" y="225" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#134e4a">Repeated Measurements & Mean Uncertainty</text></svg>

narration.script: Record all three deterministic stopwatch trials, calculate their mean, and enter the half-range uncertainty.

keyIdeas: Repeating measurements reduces random error and quantifies spread via half-range.

commonMisconceptions: Using full range instead of half-range

interactive.title: Calculate Mean Time & Half-Range Uncertainty
interactive.instructions: Click Record Trial 3 times (12.0 s, 12.2 s, 12.4 s), then enter the mean and half-range uncertainty.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Repeated stopwatch trials and mean calculation
interactive.fallbackText: Trials 12.0 s, 12.2 s, 12.4 s give mean 12.2 s ± 0.2 s.

slides.title: 15. Precision, Significant Figures & Non-Visual Equivalent
slides.purpose: Cambridge AS precision formatting, half-least-count uncertainty, and accessible non-visual equivalent assessment.
onScreenText: Match decimal places to instrument resolution
Half-least-count uncertainty for a 0.1 cm ruler is ±0.05 cm

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="225" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Precision, Significant Figures & Accessibility</text></svg>

narration.script: Record the length to 3 significant figures with its half-least-count uncertainty, or switch to the non-visual equivalent question.

keyIdeas: Trailing zeros like 10.0 cm communicate real measurement precision (3 s.f.).

commonMisconceptions: Dropping trailing zeros on exact scale marks

interactive.title: Record to 3 Significant Figures with Half-Least-Count Uncertainty
interactive.instructions: Enter the length to 3 significant figures (1 d.p.) and its ±0.05 cm uncertainty.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Ruler precision and significant figures simulation
interactive.fallbackText: The reference block measures 10.0 cm ± 0.05 cm (3 significant figures).

nonVisualQuestion.prompt: A centimetre ruler has smallest divisions of 0.1 cm. An object aligns exactly with the 10 cm mark. How should the measurement and half-least-count uncertainty be recorded?
nonVisualQuestion.explanation: A 0.1 cm ruler supports 1 decimal place (10.0 cm, 3 s.f.) with half-least-count uncertainty ±0.05 cm.
